utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Tribunal against Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic, also know as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Before we start with our next witness, I gather that the Prosecutor suggested a different list of witnesses for this week. Actually, it is stated here it's for the week 24th to 28th of September, but probably you mean August. All right. I assume this document has also been provided to the parties and the court would need two more copies. The second point is that in going through the various witness statements over the weekend, I realised that one -- I will call it by number, the -- yes. Number 12, the witness statement for number 12, witness number 12 in the old list, the list on page 6, paragraph 5, of the document filed by the Prosecution on the 19th of August, it is now witness 8 in the new list which we have just received. Now, we have received a statement of two pages, followed by a statement made by a different witness, so there is a mix up, and in spite of the pagination, which is correct. I don't know whether this applies also to the Defence. We have, in any case, received a document which is the sort of a mix up of two different statements, so, therefore, none of them is complete. Also, we don't have a statement relating to witness number 8 in the old list, and it's witness number -- no, it has disappeared from the new list. Number 8 on the old list, there is no statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: No, number 8 is not going to be testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Oh, has dropped out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. If there are no other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have -- we do have another matter that we'd like to take up before the first witness appears, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This matter relates to the incident that happened on Friday with the protected witness. We have filed, just this morning, a request that the Trial Chamber issue an order prohibiting further disclosure of that name from anyone who was in the gallery at the time the name was mentioned, and any media who may have been in the gallery at the time the name was mentioned. The proposed language is, of course, our proposal, but we have provided that in a request that the Chamber should be getting at any moment. I'll be happy to read off the language that we are proposing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please, because I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: "The Trial Chamber of the ICTY, noting that on 20 August, 1998, the Prosecutor applied to this Trial Chamber for protective measures on behalf of a witness scheduled to appear at that time, noting that all counsel for the accused acquiesced in that request, noting that on that date this Trial Chamber issued an order designed to protect the identity of that witness, noting that this witness did, in fact, testify before this Trial Chamber as a protected witness on 20 August, 1998; considering that on the following day, 21 August, 1998, the identity of that protected witness was disclosed in open session by Mr. Radovic, Defence counsel for one of the accused, during his cross-examination of another witness; noting that this Trial Chamber, upon recognising the disclosure, acted as quickly as possible by immediately ordering the appropriate redactions; noting however that disclosure was made in an open session at which members of the public and media may have been present or were present; whereas it is essential --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel, slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Sorry. ... whereas it is essential to the safety and security of this witness that his or her identity not be revealed; and whereas it is crucial to the integrity of these proceedings that the protection provided to witnesses by the Trial Chamber be scrupulously observed so that persons with relevant evidence for the Prosecution or for the Defence, in this case as well as in all other cases, will not hesitate to come forward out of fear for their well-being, orders the media and members of the public not to further publish or disclose in any way the identity of the protected witness named by Defence counsel during cross-examination on 21 August, 1998. And that would be the proposed language in the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. I understand that we may order the media not to publish or disclose anything about the identity of this protected witness, but what about the members of the public? We don't even know who was there. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think the Court has the authority to order members of the public, who inadvertently -- who happened to be present and heard the name, to obey the protection order that this court imposed for the witness. I think it's difficult to enforce such an order against a member of the public, but I take the position that the public will have great respect for this court's order and will obey it, and the media as well, I believe, will do so. But in any event, I think there is really not much else that can be done to try to prevent further damage, and so we take the position that it would be a useful thing to do to issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecutor keeps referring to my slip of the tongue during the cross-examination of the witness. However, it is interesting to note that the counsel is requesting redaction and protective measures regarding this witness during my cross-examination. However, on page 348, the name was already mentioned, on 348 of the transcript, but the Prosecutor requested redaction much later, even though the name was mentioned during the testimony of witness Ahmic Abdulah. So I don't see the difference between mentioning the name on Friday and mentioning the name during the testimony of Abdulah Ahmic. So it appears that the witness is in jeopardy only because of my cross-examination and that he was not in danger during the testimony of Abdulah Ahmic. So I do not understand the position of the Prosecution. Also, I can claim with certainty that after the testimony of any witness here, nothing happened to any witness in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Of course, I am not opposed to what the Prosecutor is saying, I'm just drawing your attention to lack of consistency in his approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajina, briefly, please, so that we don't spend too much time on this procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I would like to address the Court on a different matter once we close on this point, that is why I just raise my hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let me ask Mr. Moskowitz about this inconsistency at page 348. I don't have transcript close at hand so I can't check. Any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, we have a comment on that, and I think it really goes to the heart of our concern about what happened on Friday. We certainly recognise the possibility of slips of the tongue. In fact, my recollection is that perhaps Ms. Glumac, at one point, inadvertently had a slip of the tongue, and it can happen to anyone, and we understand that. I think we were so concerned about what happened on Friday because our feeling was that this was perhaps more than a slip of the tongue, and we went back and checked the transcript of what happened, and it appears to reinforce that feeling. The testimony, as we know, did not appear to have any relationship with the protected the witness's prior testimony, first of all. Second of all, the question had to do with pointing out an inconsistency of some sort, and certainly that could be done by simply saying, "We have had testimony here about such and such, what do you say about that?" An unfair question in this case, since there was no inconsistency given the time lapse between the two witness, but leave that be. Instead, Mr. Radovic prefaced his question at some length with, "Do you know a person," and gave the profession, gave the country from which this person came, then gave his name. That was serious, but perhaps not so serious until the next thing happened, and that is when the witness indicated some uncertainty about who this person was, as if that was important in any event. Mr. Radovic then says this witness, who was a protected witness, that is he appeared in this court as a protected witness and testified, so and so and so. Now, I fail to see what purpose that served, except to in some way publish the fact that a protected witness testified in this court. It is hard for us to see that as a slip of the tongue, and it leaves us with the impression either that it was deliberate, or that it was reckless or negligent, and under either situation would have grave concerns about the ability of Mr. Radovic to remain as an officer of this court. And I say that with great caution and sadness, because I consider Mr. Radovic an extremely able attorney, and that, I think, is one of the reasons why we are concerned. He is able, he knows how to put questions. That has been clear to everyone. He is a good cross-examiner. This is not good cross-examination. This appears to be going far afield to publish for some reason, or to demonstrate such reckless disregard for this court's order that it puts into question his ability to continue to obey this court's orders. Now, we have other witnesses coming in here this week who expect to be protected, and we have grave concerns whether an attorney who has shown such disregard for the Court's orders in the past will continue to do so in the future. And I would also add that we have an obligation to the witness to alert him to the fact that his identity had been disclosed, and we contacted the Bosnian authorities in order to convey that information to the witness. We have been told that the witness was, in fact, informed, he is extremely upset, he feels that his safety and his well-being has been compromised on the very following day that he testified, and he has written a letter asking for an inquiry as to the circumstances behind that disclosure. I think that request is reasonable. We think that this court, in fact, has an obligation to do that, that these orders, particularly protective orders, go to the very heart of the ability of this Tribunal to secure evidence in order to arrive at a just conclusion. If those orders are recklessly, if not deliberately, disobeyed, it is a very, very serious matter that goes beyond even the safety of an individual's life or career, or the well-being of his family, it really goes to the very heart of how this Tribunal functions, and I think any Defence attorney, any Prosecutor, who takes on the obligation to appear before this Tribunal is an officer of this court, and must obey the orders and must not conduct himself in such a way as to be reckless and negligent in following those orders. Yes, slips of the tongue are excusable. This appears to be far from a slip of the tongue, and it must, I think, be looked at seriously, investigated seriously, and a fact of some sort must be determined as to the circumstances surrounding this. Otherwise, it becomes, I think, very difficult for the Prosecutor to look a witness in the eye and say, "Yes, you will protected, don't worry." It becomes difficult for us to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will decide on this matter in due course and make a ruling, but for the time being, let me remind all parties that we have Rule 77, which states in item (a): "Any person who discloses information relating to proceedings in knowing violation of an order of the Chamber, commits a contempt of the Tribunal." Let me remind, you therefore, that we have this important rule and we intend to apply it consistently. If there is any repetition of this event. Now, I suggest, as I say, we, for the time being, we move on to other matters, and let me ask Mr. Krajina to make his point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, may I be allowed to address the Court in order to clarify a procedural matter having to do with the calling of witnesses. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, the office of the Prosecution has submitted a list of witness that is it intends to call as Prosecution witnesses, and as far as I have understood, they have intimated the possibility of calling other witnesses who are not on the list. As the Defence of the accused Vlatko Kupreskic intend to call certain witnesses that the Prosecution may have an interest in, we would like to protect those witnesses in such a way as to announce them as Defence witnesses and ask the Trial Chamber to forbid contact with those witnesses of ours, if I may call them that, without our permission, in the same way as the trial Chamber ruled regarding the Prosecution request, and, quite correctly, prevented us from establishing contact with Prosecution witnesses. Our interest is that these witnesses remain Defence witnesses so that the Prosecution only has the right to cross-examine them after our examination-in-chief. So we would like to appeal to the time Chamber to instruct us as to the manner in which we should proceed, and we are ready to provide the trial Chamber and the Prosecution with a list of those witnesses, and we also have the necessary evidence to show that those witnesses have confirmed their willingness to come to court and testify as defence witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Of course we consider that we are not entitled to ask the Prosecutor to close their list of witnesses. Under our rules, they have the right to call witnesses even during the trial. So, therefore, the best way -- but we do appreciate your problem, and we are sensitive to your concerns. So our suggestion is that you should provide the Court and Prosecution with the list of witnesses you intend to call and then we will decide what to do, if there are any witnesses common to both the Defence and Prosecution, we can decide on that matter. So as soon as possible, if you could kindly give us a list of the witnesses you intend to call. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we are now in a position to move on to our first witness, and I wonder whether Prosecution could call Witness B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Witness B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And what are the protected measures envisaged for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Face protection and name protection. So he will have his face blocked out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Not his voice?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Not his voice (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. We have decided to call you Witness B. May I ask you to read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would ask the usher, at this time, to hand this exhibit to Witness B, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 62. THE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness B, you have requested protection measures, and they have been granted, so I wanted to just make sure you knew that, and you may feel free to testify. Now, could you tell us your age, please?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Thirty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And could you give us just a little bit of your background, your schooling, if you would, just so we have that understanding?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Ahmici and Vitez, military secondary school in Belgrade, the military academy in Belgrade and Banja Luka. That is my background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When you completed the military training in Belgrade, would that have been in about 1984, so we have a sense of timing here?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then after your military training in Belgrade, you joined the JNA, the National Army of Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And rose through the ranks of the JNA to the rank of Captain, is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And left the JNA in 1991 when Yugoslavia began to break up and returned to Central Bosnia in that year?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. Only if I may add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I was in the barracks in Zagreb, and I left it in August 1991 because I didn't want to participate in the war against the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, when you returned to Central Bosnia, where did you go to work and what was your job?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: By orders of the Presidency of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we were supposed to report to the Territorial Defence headquarters. I reported to the headquarters in Vitez, the Defence headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And that would have been in about 1991, sometime during the summer?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I didn't report immediately. A bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, at the time you reported to the Territorial Defence in Vitez, could you tell us what the situation was at the TO regarding Croats and Muslims? Were they working together or were they working separately?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We were working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have a common enemy at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And that would be the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your function was at the Territorial Defence headquarters in Vitez during that time period when you were all working together?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I was the person responsible for security. If I can explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Certainly. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It had to do with dealing with any conflicts that may occur within the Municipality of Vitez. I had to provide security for the staff commander, the collection of information and data within the Municipality of Vitez and from the frontlines towards the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you in uniform during this time period?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you armed during this time period?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was the Territorial Defence in Vitez located in a particular building at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when Croat members of the TO split off and established their own headquarters and their own organisation separate from the joint operation that you had when you first arrived in 1991?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you remember about when that was, and I know it's sometimes difficult to recall specific days, but give us a general ball park figure, if you can?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened in the spring? Why was there a split, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The Croats set up a parallel headquarters, which they called the Stozer, in the hotel. I couldn't tell you why they separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would this have been the Hotel Vitez where the Croats established their headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What did they call themselves? Did they change their name from the TO to something else; do you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: They called themselves the main headquarters of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What does the HVO mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time, I would ask the usher, if he would, to show the witness formerly entered Exhibit P7 and then we will be asking him to look at Exhibit P9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that depicts, Exhibit P7?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It is a panorama view of the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: It's a little bit, I think, difficult to distinguish individual buildings, and so it may be unfair to ask you to try to do that. But to the best of your ability, could you show us, if it's on this aerial view, the building in which the combined Territorial Defence was located before there was this split in '92? There's a pointer right there you can use.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I can. This building, this one here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you show us the building where the HVO had their headquarters in the spring or the summer of '92, the Hotel Vitez, to the best of your ability?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, before there was this split, you say you worked together with Croats. Did you work well with them? Was there a good relationship or was it a bad relationship, a strained one?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It was a strained relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At that time, do you remember any of the names of the individual Croats who you worked with on a frequent basis, before the split?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Zeljko Sajevic, Livancic, Rebac. We collaborated well with Ivan Santic. The chief was Pero Skopljak, Mario Cerkez. These were all people that we cooperated with. I want to say the following, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: While we had common interests and the same enemy, it can be said that we worked well in this building. This one here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That was the building where you were together jointly for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But at the same time, they already had a section in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did there come a time that the TO that was left after the Croats moved to the -- after the HVO moved to the Hotel Vitez, did there come a time that the TO that was left had to move out of that original building and go somewhere else, and if so, could you show us where?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. We had to leave that building by orders of the HVO. We had to move out, the MUP was beneath us, the police, and we moved out to a house, here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know why the HVO made it necessary for you to move the TO to that house from the public building where it was formerly located?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I think that at that time already the HVO engaged in certain ploys, and the commander, Hakija Cengic, attended a meeting in the hotel, and he was told about this. I don't know the reason; I just know that we moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can the usher, if he would, show the P9 exhibit at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us what P9 shows?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The Vitez Hotel in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And that is the hotel you were talking about where the HVO centred its operations in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that the Muslim or Bosniak TO then that was left had to move to a house. Were there any Croats that moved with you, that stayed with you, or did all the Croats initially go to the HVO at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Some Croats stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any of them who stayed for a while?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: For about another month there was Zeljko Sajevic, Blazenko Ramljak, a lady and her daughter, I can't recall the name now, then Vlatko Males, Anto Furundzija, Dragan Calic, Nenad Palavra, and another one, but I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mentioned Anto Furundzija as one of the Croats who stayed with the TO for a period of time, I think you said a month. Did you come to know Anto Furundzija fairly well during this time period?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you on a fairly friendly relationship at this time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, after the split and after the move to that house, did you come to know a man by the name of Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us who Vlado Santic was in 1992 when you got to know him? What was his position, rank, and duties, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't know his rank, what rank he had, but his duties were, he was the commander of the HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did the HVO military police have a sort of particular kind of uniform that was easily identifiable?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you describe it, please?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: They wore a camouflage uniform with white belts, a white holder for their pistol. They had a badge which they wore on their jackets, it was in black leather with a metal badge indicating the words "Military Police" and the number of that particular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the sort of functions and duties of the HVO military police at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The HVO police, just as any other police, was intended to protect the law. It was meant to protect the citizens, the constitution of the country. This police, the HVO police, maintained checkpoints, and it ensured security for the headquarters. It arrested Bosniaks, it seized trucks carrying humanitarian aid heading towards Tuzla, Zavidovici, Visoko. They did everything that was against the Bosniaks. They were supposed to investigate every murder. Not a single murder was properly investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At that time, were you receiving complaints in your official capacity as a security officer? Were you receiving complaints from citizens about mistreatment that they were receiving from either the military HVO or Croat citizens that you felt were not being properly investigated by the police?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I know you've mentioned a couple of things already about what should have been investigated, but if you could just give us an idea of the kinds of complaints that you were receiving during this time period, and we're talking, I think, after the split in '92, the kinds of complaints that you would be getting from people so that we have a general understanding of what was going on then?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In the Vitez Hotel, a Bosniak called Trako was killed. Myself and Ivan Santic were at the funeral, and this murder was never elucidated even though it was well-known that Mario Cerkez was in the hotel at that particular moment. In the village of Nadioci, in the most brutal manner, a Bosniak called Esad Salkic was killed. His house was blown up. I went to the site. He was killed by Miroslav Bralo, known as Cicko, but they, the HVO, that is Vlado Santic, never cooperated in investigating this matter, nor anyone else from the HVO. Neither Pasko, neither Cerkez, neither Pero Skopljak. There were daily incidents at the checkpoint, particularly the checkpoint near the Impregnacija company. I could show it you on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would this be the area near the Dubravica --

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where the mountain road to Zenica meets the valley road?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct. There was a checkpoint at Divjak, there was a checkpoint at the bend of the road going to Travnik, Novi Travnik, another one at Kaonik, another checkpoint in Lasva. There were checkpoints all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: These are HVO checkpoints you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: All of them were HVO. There was not a single Bosniak checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What kind of complaints were you receiving about these checkpoints from Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Bosniaks were stopped there, they were taunted, they were insulted and cursed at, their money was seized from them. They confiscated their cars, lorries. At night, they would shoot, especially during the night and especially in the area of Ahmici. They would throw grenades. All this was meant to provoke the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, having received these kinds of complaints on a daily basis, did you, in your official capacity, come to know Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, frequently contact Vlado Santic regarding these complaints?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did you make contact with him? Was it face to face or by the telephone or by letter?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It was both face to face and by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What precisely was your purpose in making these contacts with Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I was a person representing the Territorial Defence staff and I was in charge of contacts for resolving conflict situations with the HVO. When I asked for Pero Skopljak from the HVO or Mario Cerkez, who were commanders, they would refer me to Vlado Santic. I would establish telephone contact with him or I would agree on a meeting at the hotel or we would solve matters over the phone or, rather, try to resolve them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And the matters you're referring to are these complaints that you were receiving, I take it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, ever -- were you ever successful in having Vlado Santic, to your satisfaction, resolve any of these issues despite your meetings with him both by phone and in person?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: By the way, you talked about meeting Vlado Santic face to face. Where would meet him? Would it be in your home or his home or would it be in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And would you meet in some public area or would it be privately in his office?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, we talk about the Hotel Vitez. At this time, was this really a hotel in any sense of the word, or was it simply taken over by the HVO in total for their headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: That hotel lost its hotel function. The hotel was closed to the general public, especially for Bosniaks. It was the headquarters of the HVO. The restaurant that used to exist here on the left was the canteen for the commanders and soldiers of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the general public, particularly Bosniaks, were not allowed into the hotel. How did you get into the hotel to see Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: First, I would like to add something, if I may. The hotel had barbed wire -- a barbed-wire fence around it. Certain parts, especially on the other side, were roofed over with timber, the windows to the offices. The entrance was on the side of the petrol station, and there was an entrance from the side where the post office is. To enter the hotel, I would ring up before that and agree on a meeting and announce my arrival. At the entrance to the hotel there were soldiers, and when I said that I had an appointment, they would know about it and they would let me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you recall a time when you were in Vlado Santic's office where you saw your former colleague Anto Furundzija? Do you recall a time like that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We're wondering whether you need to put questions about Furundzija, who is accused in a different trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, Mr. President, we do feel it is relevant to this case and particularly to Mr. Santic, because it connects to the Jokers unit which participated in the massacre in Ahmici, and, therefore, ties in Vlado Santic as an aider and abettor through that connection. So we do feel it's important to show the connection between Santic and the Jokers, and I will have additional evidence later to tie in that connection even more tightly. So this is preparatory to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moskowitz, a moment. Furundzija is being tried in another case by this Trial Chamber. Now, if you are proposing to call evidence prejudicial to him, I think we need to consider that, because he's not here and he's not represented. So is there a way in which you could deal with this without reference to him specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm not sure if there is a way to do that. It is, of course, true that he is not represented, and, therefore, any evidence that comes into this case with reference to Mr. Furundzija, in my view, cannot be used against him in the other case. Yes, it is before this trial Chamber, but I think this Trial Chamber is fully capable of, compartmentalising that evidence, and certainly Mr. Furundzija should not be held accountable for any evidence that comes into this case with reference to him. Unfortunately, in this case, in order to tie Vlado Santic into the crimes in Ahmici and in order to make some sense of the later testimony, the connection between Santic and Furundzija, I'm afraid, is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have decided that you may proceed, however, it should be clear that whatever evidence is produced which may affect Mr. Furundzija will not be regarded as evidence in the case against Furundzija because he is not here and is not represented, as Judge May pointed out. So we will disregard what evidence is produced relating to Furundzija. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: The question, again, is: Do you recall a time when you were talking with Vlado Santic in his office in the way that you've described, that you did frequently, when you saw your former colleague, Furundzija, at the Hotel Vitez? And if you recall that, could you tell us and describe, if you would, the circumstances surrounding that meeting?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. I was sitting in the office talking to Santic about two cars that had been confiscated from Bosniaks and negotiating on their return. Anto Furundzija opened the door, he was wearing a uniform, carrying a pistol and a gun. His face was masked with cream. He was holding a helmet in his hand. When he saw me he was taken aback. He said, "Good day," and I responded, and he told Santic, "It's all right, we're back." At the same time, I saw quite a few soldiers passing down the corridor. They were all sweaty and their faces were painted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Santic indicated anything back to Anto Furundzija at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, yes. He asked, "How did it go? Is everything all right?" And he said they should put away their equipment and lunch would be ready soon, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you form an opinion at that time, as you observed the two men together, Furundzija and Santic, did you form an opinion as to the command relationship between those two men?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. I thought they were in a command relationship, that they were connected, because both of them were wearing white belts, white belts, which is a sign of belonging to the same unit or a similar unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And did you form an opinion as to who was the superior of the other?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It's my opinion, but I'm not certain, that at that moment, at that moment, Santic was the superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, during this time period, and again referring to 1992, did you have occasion to frequently visit Ahmici, the village of Ahmici, for personal reasons, and don't go into those reasons at this point, but answer yes or no if that's true?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And in order to -- by the way, you were not living in Ahmici at that time, were you?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: But in a village not far away; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And you would often, I assume, go from Vitez to Ahmici in order to make those visits; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: In order to go from Vitez to Ahmici, did you have to pass any checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And tell us where these checkpoints were, or if only one, where that one was?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Depending on the time when I was going there, when times were, let us say, normal, there was a checkpoint at Impregnacija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That's the one of which you spoke of earlier near the Dubravica school area?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was always a checkpoint there. That one was never taken down. And the others were set up depending on the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This may be a little bit awkward, and I'm not sure it's possible, I haven't checked in advance with the usher, so I apologise for that, but just for clarity's sake, it might be useful to demonstrate where this Dubravica area is. We have that large aerial in the back. I could easily ask the witness to proceed to that aerial and show Vitez, show Ahmici, and then show where the Dubravica checkpoint was, if that is permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand, however, that he if goes there his face cannot be distorted, so therefore, we can't protect him. The Registrar is suggesting that after the break they could move here the big picture so that he may identify the relevant point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you recall a time during one of your trips to Ahmici that you ran into or met with Mr. Furundzija, your former colleague?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It was at the Dubravica checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: On that day, did you actually go through the checkpoint, or did you stop before the checkpoint or were you stopped at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: At the checkpoint was always a very strong checkpoint. It was a dug-out machine-gun nest. There were obstacles. I avoided going to Ahmici on a daily basis because of that checkpoint, but I had to. And I wanted to see what the situation at the checkpoint was, and to test the reaction. Once, in the autumn of 1992, when I was taking a trip there, I saw that there was some problems before I arrived at the checkpoint. There were many soldiers, there was a truck that had been stopped. Of course, it was a Bosniak truck carrying humanitarian aid to Kakanj. I was on my way from Vitez, and I stopped some 20 metres away from the checkpoint before I reached it. At the same time, from the other side, from the direction of Ahmici, Anto Furundzija arrived. He passed through and stopped at the point where I was. I was standing beside my car, he approached me and we greeted one another. That's where we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation at that time, you and Mr. Furundzija?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What do you recall about that conversation?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I asked him, "What's this," at the checkpoint, and he replied that he didn't know either. Since we had been in the Territorial Defence staff together and I know that he joined the HVO later, I asked him, "Where are you now?" First, let me say that he was wearing a uniform with a white belt, and he had a pistol case which was slung low. He was wearing it like a cowboy. He said he was now the commander of a special unit based in the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You referred to a place called the Bungalow. Did you understand what he meant by the Bungalow, and could you tell us where that is?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. The Bungalow is a motel close to Ahmici. It's a place we used to go swimming, because there was a river close by at the place called Seliste. The village of Nadioci is there. I can show it on the map if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think we'll probably arrange the demonstration of the map for a later time but, yes, we will ask you to do that when we can establish the proper technology. What was Mr. Furundzija's sort of demeanour or attitude as he was talking to you about his new command, at the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, you know, he was a young man, and he was now in a situation where he was the boss, where he was the commander of a unit, and as such he was full of himself. He was very arrogant. He was driving cars, he had an escort, and I think that because of all this he was rather naive and he said a lot of things, because he didn't know what would happen later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the first conflict that occurred in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I apologise, but I wouldn't call it a conflict at all. I would call it the first attack of the HVO of Central Bosnia against the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you in Ahmici during that first attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you part of the command decision to set up a barricade in Ahmici? Did you take part in that decision?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Again, I wouldn't call this a barricade, I would prefer to call it an obstruction of the road, and I did not participate in making this decision and I did not command or make any decisions. There were superiors above me who did that. It was up to me only to gather as much information as possible and take it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This may be a good point to take the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We rise now for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be allowed to ask a question linked to the problem of witness protection because we are going to hear three to four protected witnesses now, and the Prosecutor has mentioned my name too as having disclosed the name of one of the witnesses, and this has been done by colleague Radovic as well, and I see that the letter addressed by Bosnia-Herzegovina mentions us as well. I just wanted to clear up this point. I understand that I must not disclose the identity of a witness, but he was one of the factual witnesses and we have to establish his relevance and the events linked to him. Therefore, we are in a position to have to use his name, and I think that we should be allowed to do that as part of the cross-examination but, of course, we mustn't mention his identity as a witness in this trial because he is protected only as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: It seems to me that if Defence counsel feel it necessary to mention a protected witness's name, we could go into closed session at that point, and it's merely a matter of Defence counsel seeking the indulgence of the Court to do so. On that point as well, I think I sort of made our position clear that it was our view that this was not intentional or reckless behaviour on Mrs. Glumac's part and we don't raise any issue in that regard, and we see it as quite a different issue with respect to Mr. Radovic. Mr. Radovic also, I think, made the argument that there was an inconsistent position being taken by the Prosecutor in that when Mrs. Glumac mentioned the name of the witness, there was nothing done about it, and having checked the record, that is simply not true. When the slip was made, I remember now vividly doing something rather awkward and interrupting the proceedings and asking for a little more protection than perhaps we needed, having been a little unfamiliar with the procedure myself, but we did attempt, and I think succeed, in redacting the record with regard to those names. So I think there is no inconsistent position that we are taking at all, and I think the difference between Mrs. Glumac and Mr. Radovic merely underscores our concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. But I think that we could stick to your suggestion; namely, that whenever the Defence counsel feel that it is necessary to mention the name of a witness, they can ask to go into a closed session and then we can go into a closed session so that they may be allowed to disclose those names. Is that fine with you, Mrs. Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. But I would like to put another question. Actually, there will be more protected witnesses in the future. In fact, a large number of them, judging by the list, and we agree with that in principle. But the situation was such that this witness was not a protected witness. He became a protected witness by the ruling of the Court. So what will we do with the witnesses who may appear this week or next week so we may not mention them either? So we find ourselves in a very difficult situation. How are we going to verify any fact? We will have to see whether the Prosecution intends to protect the witness later on because I mentioned the name also in this case before that witness became a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought a solution would lie in getting from the Prosecution every week a list of the witnesses they intend to call with, as they did this week, this morning we received a good document, also with the indication of whether or not any particular witness would be a protected witness and, if so, what sort of protection they are seeking for that witness. So if probably a week in advance, you will receive this list and we can advance. This may probably meet your needs. We can't rule in abstracto on this matter. Let us proceed on a pragmatic basis, so as to take into account your needs and your concerns and your demands and also the need to protect the witnesses. All right? Let's go back to our witness. If the Prosecution want to ask him to identify particular places on the map, I understand from the registry we need to go into a closed session, if only for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be helpful to the Court for him to do that, and I realise, as I was thinking about some of the questions that I think must be asked of this witness, that there may be additional questions that would tend to reveal his identity merely through his answers to those questions; specifically, his relationships to other people, which are relevant, I think, for his testimony. Maybe this would be a good time, while we are in closed session, to pose those questions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we move into closed session right away or later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Right away. All right. Now, the registrar will make sure that we are in closed session. Are we now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand we are now in closed session, so you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 25 (redacted) 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, we left off with the first conflict or the first attack, as you refer. Did you continue to make personal visits to the village of Ahmici following that first attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: During one of those personal visits, were you prevented from taking the road into Ahmici by a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you describe where that checkpoint was and who was manning it?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Shall I just speak or shall I stand up and point at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just speak.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Sometime roughly -- I can't tell you exactly whether it was the seventh or eighth day after this large-scale attack on Ahmici, when the entire Bosniak population was chased out, a part of the houses destroyed, places of worship damaged, I headed for Ahmici. I was alone in a car. I was driving there. I got as far as the turn-in to Ahmici. However, the road to Ahmici was blocked. There were certain obstacles placed there. There were two soldiers armed with rifles and they stopped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened -- I'm sorry. Continue.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: They told me, while I was standing there, from Dragan Papic's house, across the fields, Dragan Papic came running and said to me that I couldn't enter the village because they had no permission to allow anyone in. I didn't want to argue with him, and I returned to Vitez and I informed the staff about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us how Mr. Papic was dressed when he informed you that you could not enter the village, that you didn't have permission to do so?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: He was in a uniform. There was a black blouse and a camouflage vest and he had a rifle, it was an old model, an M-48, like a carbine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell whether this rifle that Mr. Papic was carrying, did it have a sniper scope on it or didn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, it didn't. At the time? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is this the kind of weapon that would be easily fitted with a sniper scope and could be removed quickly and easily?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. That is, in fact, done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mention that there were two soldiers at this checkpoint. Were they also in uniform and armed?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. They were wearing camouflage uniforms. They had rifles, automatic rifles, a Kalashnikov-type rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see any other weapons nearby covering that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: On the main road going towards Busovaca, a little further down, there was a kind of shelter, kind of small bunker with obstacles and nothing else. There was the stop sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see any machine guns in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: On that day, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned personal visits to Ahmici. After that particular visit to Ahmici, when you were stopped from going into the village by soldiers and by Dragan Papic, did you return on an official visit later on?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us about that first official visit and how that came about?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The first official visit occurred roughly after two weeks, 14 days, something like that. We were working on the return of Bosniaks to Ahmici. A representative of the International Red Cross came to the Vitez hotel. Pero Skopljak called Sefkija and told him that someone should come, that these people wanted to go to Ahmici to see what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: By "these people" you mean the representatives of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I went to the hotel together with Faud Kaknjo, who was the representative of the political body. We entered Marijan Skopljak's office in the hotel, Pero Skopljak, Mario Cerkez, Faud Kaknjo, myself and a representative of the International Red Cross. After a discussion, we headed for Ahmici. Pero Skopljak took us to the Catholic cemetery first. Allegedly he wanted to indicate that the Bosniaks had put up very strong resistance there using heavy weapons and that the tombstones had been destroyed. We looked and looked, and we didn't find a single tombstone that had been destroyed. He probably felt embarrassed that at least one of them hadn't destroyed one just to prove his point. We then returned to the school, or rather, we went as far as the religious building, the mosque. This is the mosque next to the school, the one with the minaret. It was very badly damaged. It was obvious that these were not bullets from rifles but, rather, shells from guns. Then we went on a little further upwards, as far as roughly the houses where I used to live. Then we returned, we went to the village of Tolovici, and from there we returned to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mentioned going to the mosque. In order to do that, you would have had to take the road into Ahmici, which the day before, or earlier, you said had been blocked. How were you able to get into the village on the day the Red Cross was there? Was there a checkpoint in place at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, there wasn't a checkpoint there. It's generally known why there wasn't a checkpoint there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Why do you think there wasn't a checkpoint there at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: From the Vitez headquarters of the HVO, they told the commanders of the checkpoint to remove the checkpoint so that international forces would not see that it was the Croats manning the checkpoint there, because, of course, they always wanted to say that the Bosniaks were the ones who were shooting, attacking, and on all occasions it was the Bosniaks who were driven away and whose houses were burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you recall your next official visit to Ahmici after the Red Cross visit, and tell us how that came about?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. The visit by the International Red Cross yielded a result in the sense of reconciliation. So we agreed that on the following day, we would go and visit the very spot on the ground. In the meantime, the people who would pass by on the Zenica/Busovaca road or coming down from Ahmici and who were able to see said that there was a checkpoint there. I rang up the hotel, and we agreed that we should go there to Ahmici, with the aim of taking down the checkpoint. I went there in a car of the Lada make, with the driver, Mario Cerkez. We met at the petrol station near the hotel and we went to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you ride in separate automobiles or did you ride with Mr. Cerkez in his automobile?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We went in separate cars, in separate cars. I -- we didn't -- well, we weren't rich, so we had an old Lada which was left over from the TO, the Territorial Defence headquarters, and they already had luxury cars. We arrived in Ahmici. In Ahmici there was a checkpoint. The checkpoint was located from the road to Ahmici toward Papic's house about 15 or 20 metres, where there is a widening of the road for a bus-stop. There were obstacles there, the metal cross-shaped obstacles for tanks, and there was a dugout with sandbags there, and in the dugout was an M-72 light machine-gun. There were about seven soldiers there. Nenad Antic was there. I stopped my vehicle here to the left at the entrance to Ahmici. Mario Cerkez got out of his car and he had Dragan Papic and Nenad Santic in his car. They were about 30 metres away from me, and I couldn't hear what they were talking about. Cerkez was wearing a uniform, Nenad Santic was wearing civilian clothes, and Dragan Papic was wearing a uniform. The soldiers had guns. After their conversation, Dragan Papic ordered the soldiers to remove the checkpoint. They removed the checkpoint. Cerkez only told me, "It's all right, there will be no problems," and he said nothing else. After that, they all went to the yard toward Dragan Papic's house, and I went back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mentioned there was a light machine-gun. Can you give us an idea of how big or how light this particular machine-gun was?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: A light machine-gun was not a heavy weapon. It was the kind of light machine-gun produced in Kargojevic (Phoen). A little bigger than a automatic rifle, but it's barrel is a little longer and it had a stand, and a round of 30 bullets can be put in. It can be carried by one soldier in the same way that a soldier carries a gun-- a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So this was an extremely mobile weapon which could be moved around quite easily by even one soldier then; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that Dragan Papic and the other soldiers went into the Papic house. Did you see what happened to the machine-gun? Where did it go, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Everything was taken away, together with the weapons. They all went down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: "Down there" meaning to Mr. Papic's house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, based on what you observed out there, could you give us an idea of -- or did you form an opinion as to the command structure of the individuals present at that checkpoint, starting perhaps with Mr. Cerkez and going down and describing what you view as the command structure of the other folks who were at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: You mean at that moment at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. If, indeed, you formed an opinion and can state it here.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. All the orders, all the directives for all the checkpoints came from the hotel. There were several people there, if you go from the top who gave orders for the setting up of checkpoints. And at the checkpoint itself, Mario Cerkez was the commander. He was a commander at the chief staff of the HVO in the hotel, and he gave orders to the commander of the checkpoint. And according to what I saw, I was able to conclude that the checkpoint was under the command of the Dragan Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And what led you to conclude that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: After the conversation, when Mario Cerkez had Nenad Santic and Dragan Papic in front of him, there followed a response by Dragan Papic, who made a gesture with his arm, telling the soldiers to remove all the obstacles, to remove the checkpoint and to go into the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, after everyone, as you testified earlier, then went into Mr. Papic's house, I believe you said you did not go into Mr. Papic's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you remain in the village at that time, or did you return to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I can say that the gentleman did not invite me in, and after that I returned to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you recall still another official visit to Ahmici that you made at about this same time period?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It all happened very fast, because it was very important to bring the women, the children, the old men who were in the woods back to their homes which had been abandoned, because in the houses -- but I don't mean the houses, I mean in the cow sheds and the farm buildings, there were livestock, cows, sheep, and they were hungry, they had to be fed. So it was very important for the people to go back, and I wanted us to take action at once. So that we agreed that on the following day, we would go back into the field and talk to the local HVO commanders, asking them to guarantee the safety and security of the Bosniak population so that they could return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The staff contacted the HVO staff. I am referring to Sefkija, and he agreed we should visit the spot, and again, I was the one who played this role of mediation and of resolving these conflict situations as a kind of peacemaker. Pero Skopljak told me that I could go to Ahmici, that I could get to Nenad Santic's house, and we would then go together to inspect the field. Again, I got into my car, I went to Nenad Santic's house, and from there we went to Zoran Kupreskic's house. Nenad Santic, while I was at his home, told me there would be no problem, that we would now go to Zoran's, because he was the commander of that area, and that we should agree with him so that there would be no problems regarding the return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Before you go on, I would like to clarify a couple of things. Did Mr. Skopljak accompany you to Ahmici on that day that you went to Nenad Santic's house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I think he didn't. I can't remember now, but I think he did not. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And you mentioned Nenad Santic. Could you tell us who Nenad Santic was, and approximately what part of the village he lived in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Nenad Santic was the Commander in Chief of the area gravitating from Vitez toward Santici, Zume, Ahmici. I don't know what they called it, but he was the Commander in Chief of the HVO in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Nenad Santic's house, and perhaps you could describe at this point approximately where in the village that house is located, but when you arrived at his house, what did he tell you? First tell us where the house is, and then tell us what kind of conversation you had with Mr. Santic.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The house? I would have to get up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Perhaps if you just try to describe it now, and maybe at the end of your testimony we can go back into closed session and you can point out a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, this is Santici, then there is a bend in the road and then it's to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand we are moving into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Are we in closed session now then?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us the gist of the conversation that you had with Mr. Santic at his home that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I didn't go into the house. The conversation took place in front of the house. He knew that I was coming, because they had told him from Vitez that I was coming. And he only said, "Well, I'll come out now and we'll go and visit the other commanders in the field, and we'll sit down with them when we get there."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then where did you proceed after that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: After that, we went to Zoran Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you go alone or were you accompanied by Mr. Santic and others?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We went together but separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And what did you do when you arrived in your car at the home of Zoran Santic -- I'm sorry, Zoran Kupreskic. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Zoran Kupreskic knew we were coming, because he had been told either by telephone or radio receiver. We arrived at the house, and we said, "Good day," and we went into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And can you tell us the basic conversation that occurred inside the house of Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We sat down inside the house. Nenad Santic explained the purpose of our visit, and said that we had come with the aim of returning or making it possible for the Bosniaks to return, and that Zoran should provide security and guarantee that there would be no problems on the occasion of the return of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons inside Zoran Kupreskic's house while you were there?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What did you see and where was it in the house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: There's a staircase when you go in and then you turn right, and in the corridor, in a corner near the door, there was a rifle and an army pack and helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall how Mr. Kupreskic reacted to the statement from Nenad Santic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: He reacted positively and he promised there would be no problems. He even expressed regret that all this had occurred, and he said that he personally would take action to make sure there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where did you and the others go after that meeting was concluded?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: After that, we went to Ivica Kupreskic's house, which is about 50 metres away from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is that house basically across the road from Zoran Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what transpired in Ivica Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We sat down on the terrace of the house and we talked about the same topic as before in the house of Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was the reaction from Ivica the same as Zoran's?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and he promised that -- they had promised that they would take away the landmines which had been set up in the direction of Pirici and in the upper part of Ahmici. They had their guards, their patrols, up there in certain places. They said they would withdraw all of that and that the people could start returning to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Had you known about those landmines before or was this the first that you had heard, that there were, in fact, landmines planted by the HVO and that Ivica knew about them?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, Ivica, with I don't know who, participated in placing these landmines. He probably had a certain munitions depot which included landmines and explosive devices, and I know this because a Bosniak called Meho Hrustanovic, he and his wife were also killed on the 16th of April in front of their house. After the first clash, he started out from Vrhovine towards his house, and Ivica Kupreskic probably saw him coming, he knew there were landmines there, and Ivica ran up and yelled at him to stop, to stop, not to proceed because there were landmines there, and this man went back, he went back towards another village to the north of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Moskowitz. Have you got a few more questions on this particular issue or can we stop here and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: It would be, I think, a logical place to stop in maybe five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you go to a third house on that particular visit to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Which house was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We went to Ivo Papic's house, yes. That is Dragan Papic's house, and his father is Ivo Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Whose decision was it to go to Ivo Papic's house, your decision or Nenad Santic's decision?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Nenad Santic was in charge of everything. He was the one taking me to where we were supposed to go. I didn't know who to visit, but Nenad Santic was the one who said, "Let's go to Zoran's, let's go to Ivica's, let's go to Ivo's," or Dragan Papic's house because they were living together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Tell us again what transpired at the Ivo Papic house, please?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The same. The same. I won't repeat this. We agreed on the same. The same things were agreed on, were promised, and we went back to Vitez. I reported to the commander and the staff that an agreement had been reached and that the people could go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This may be a good point to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We rise now and we will reconvene at ten past two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.37 p.m. 25 1

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you think, Mr. Moskowitz, you can conclude your examination-in-chief before the coffee break? I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I intend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would like to start off by asking the usher to show several exhibits that have already been entered into evidence to the witness, beginning with Exhibit P34.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Exhibit P34 has been placed on the ELMO machine next to you. Does that look familiar? Do those houses look familiar, and if so, could you identify them for us?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. The houses of the Kupreskics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you say which house is which?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This is Zoran Kupreskic's house and this is Ivica Kupreskic's house (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So for purposes of the record then, you're pointing to the house that appears on the right as Zoran's house and the house that appears on the left as Ivica's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, are those the two houses you went to on that day that you've described where you and Mr. Nenad Santic were going around to the commanders of Ahmici to talk about the return of the civilians after the first attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can the usher now show the witness Exhibit 30?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you identify Exhibit 30, please?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This is Ivo Papic's house or, rather, Dragan Papic lived there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You have mentioned going into that house as well with Mr. Santic --

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- to talk about the return of civilians?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've also spoken about the Hotel Vitez. Would you tell us, during this time period, and I'm talking about the time period now between the first attack and the second attack, that is, between October and April, October '92, April '93, how often did you pass by the Hotel Vitez, not enter it but pass by it on your way to and from various places?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I passed there every day, sometimes five, ten. It depended on the day. Five or ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you ever see Vlatko Kupreskic at the Hotel Vitez while you were passing by?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate of how many times you think you recall seeing Vlatko Kupreskic at the Hotel Vitez, a ball park figure?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In which period do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Well, let's take the period between the two attacks, that is, October '92 to April of '93.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Three to five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
