utterances.text: Do you recall the last time you saw him in front of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I remember that day very well. If I may, I can give you more details?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I went to the headquarters. In front of the municipality building, across the road to the hotel, there was a bus full of old people. As I knew one of them called Franjo, I asked him, "Where are you going?" And he answered, "I don't know. They just rounded us up and told us that they were taking us somewhere, to Croatia." I went on. I saw that something was in the offing, so I decided to make a tour. So I headed towards Han Bila. At a place called Zabilje, near Sadovace, which is another locality, I saw roughly 15 to 20 HVO soldiers in uniform and under arms setting up a checkpoint. I returned and I briefed my commander about these details. After that, it may have been about 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon, I know that it was overcast, I was passing by the hotel, and in front of the entrance to the hotel that we saw a photograph of a moment ago, there was Vlatko Kupreskic with another two, maybe three men in uniform. They were standing in front of the hotel. If I may also add --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: That day, the atmosphere was extremely tense because Kraljevic, his first name is Darko, Darko Kraljevic, somewhere in the surroundings of Kruscica, in the mountains, had said the day before that he had been attacked and then they arrested two Bosniaks at the checkpoint and took them away somewhere. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher, please, to show Exhibit P9 at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Exhibit P9 has been placed on the ELMO. You've already identified this as the front of the Hotel Vitez. Does this photograph show an area where you saw Vlatko Kupreskic on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you point, if you would, where you saw Vlatko Kupreskic standing?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: For the record, you're pointing at the front door of the hotel. It's a little difficult to tell. How close to the front door do you estimate he was when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It's not very far. The distance is not 30 metres. In view of the fact that I was going from the direction of Stari Vitez, so I was going along this side of the road (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you on foot or in an automobile?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you going fast or slow?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you have a good opportunity to observe him?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I saw him very well. I was alone in the car. There was nobody to block my vision. May I add ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This area here (indicating), there was intensified security here. There were soldiers. There were more soldiers there than otherwise, and I already said that everything was fenced in with barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did that barbed wire obstruct your view in any way of the front door of the hotel as you drove past?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No. No, no. It was just there to prevent entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This was sometime in the afternoon of the 15th; is that what you said? Do you know the exact time? Can you put an exact time on it, or are you estimating in the afternoon, at any time during the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: As I have already said, it was about -- it was after 1400 hours, around -- between 1400 and 1500 hours. It's difficult to pinpoint it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, one detail that I think we left out earlier when you were looking at the aerial of the downtown Vitez area was the movement of the headquarters for the Bosniak TO after the split, and I want to just clarify that now. I believe you testified that after the split, the Bosniak TO moved to a house in another part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At some point, did the headquarters of the TO move again to another building, after that?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Would that have been the school in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the secondary school. Secondary school. Next to it was the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And that subsequent to that, the headquarters moved to a building located in Stari Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. After the events in October, everything was moved to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If the usher could show Exhibit P7 again, please? This is the aerial of Vitez that you've already identified earlier in your testimony, and I forgot to ask these questions and I wanted to complete the record on this. Could you show us where the TO headquarters was just before the move to the school, just so we can get back to there?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And again, for the record, this is a very small depiction of some of the buildings in this village, but you're pointing basically to near the top of the aerial in the centre, to a small house or building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm just trying to make the record as to where you're pointing on that aerial map. Point again to the headquarters location after the split, if you would?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: After the split. A house here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And then where do the headquarters move from there? Show us where the school is.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This was one part of the headquarters. The commander and the staff were there, and in the house there was a food storage space that we kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you show us where the TO moved after the school, and where it was on the day of April 16, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It's not on the picture. It's not on this aerial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you just show us in what direction it would be if this aerial happened to show that area?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This space here is a field, and then along this road, about a hundred metres away, there is a turning to the right, and then a hundred metres along that road there's an ordinary house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And is that part of Vitez now referred to as Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: The old part of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It's called Stari Vitez. I don't know why, but that's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, where were you on April 16, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you at the headquarters of the TO or were you in a different building close by?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And what did you see and hear happening on that day, if you could just describe for us your recollections of that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, I would suggest that I describe an event that occurred the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I have already said that the day was murky in every sense of the word. As soon as the presence of the HVO troops was intensified, the Bosniaks withdrew into their homes. We -- or rather, the commander decided that all of us should stay and spend the night in that house. There was just one room, there were no facilities there. About 23.00 hours in the evening, a person from the British Battalion came to our headquarters, a Captain, Captain Matthew, and the surname starts with "D", I can't remember now. Anyway, Captain Matthew, and his surname begins with the letter "D". He was an Irishman, and he had understanding for these parts, and he wanted peace. At least that is how we saw him, as a person for peace. He came and told us that he had come to see us from the Hotel Vitez. He said that down there, Blaskic was having a meeting, a gathering of many, many men in uniform. I, and probably the commander and the others as well, thought that Mr. Blaskic had come to calm down the situation, because I said that there had been problems with Kraljevic and those two Bosniaks that I mentioned, because we requested that they return the two men, and they wouldn't and they threatened us. This meeting, as everyone knows, was actually on assignments to individuals on the basis of a plan that they already had when they sent troops for training at Zabilje. Why we didn't react, we didn't react because there had been a hundred similar situations in the past. Secondly, we never believed that they really would attack us in the way in which they actually did, because they had taken everything that could be taken. We had nothing. They had all the power, the entire territory, control of the police, everything. They controlled everything. May I now go on to the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We were in the headquarters in the early morning. It was maybe 6.00, quarter past. I don't know what time it was. We were asleep on chairs, and we heard a strong explosion. We thought that somebody had fired from a rifle, but then the shells started falling. Men started coming from the surrounding houses, telling us that HVO troops were attacking, shooting, killing, torching houses. The first to reach us was Edo Arnaut. He came to the headquarters and said, "I fled from my house. They are on their way and they are shooting." In great haste, we organised ourselves as much as we could, and put up resistance, and they didn't enter Stari Vitez. The situation regarding the other areas, we could not monitor at first. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You talked about putting up some resistance. Approximately how many armed soldiers were there for the TO in Stari Vitez resisting this attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: About 30 to 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, during this day, or perhaps it was the next day, did there come a time that a young HVO either soldier or a person associated with the HVO came into custody in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. He came in himself. He wasn't arrested in an operation, he just walked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How was it possible for someone just to walk in during this kind of attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This was only the beginning, and, of course, there were shortcomings in our defence, unprotected areas. We focused on particular axes, whereas this road was not blocked, nor did we pay any attention to it, thinking that nobody would get -- would pass and come in from that direction. However, this young man went from the hotel towards Stari Vitez. He simply entered and our people arrested him, took him into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was he questioned at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you participate in the questioning, or did you overhear the questioning or part of the questioning?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I didn't take part in the questioning. There were people -- other people who were responsible for that, but I went to see who the young man was and how they were treating him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And how were they treating him?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: He was treated in the way a prisoner of war should be treated, in accordance with the principles and guidelines of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you overhear any of the questions and answers, particularly the answers, given by this person?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What do you recall hearing?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: He was asked how come that he should have decided to come in the direction of Stari Vitez? How come he was in Stari Vitez at all when the HVO had launched an offensive along all the axes and against all the areas inhabited by Bosniaks. He was not knowledgeable. He said that he been near the hotel with the troops, that he had said the he was going to Mosunj, I think he had a sick sister there, and he had taken the road to Stari Vitez. Nobody had told him not to go there. In fact, they were laughing at him a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall him saying anything else of interest?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. I overheard a couple of other questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Go ahead and tell us what you recall about that.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: They asked him where he was from, what his name was and what he had been doing and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What did he say his name was?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Zoran Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And what did he say he had been doing?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: He said that he had spent the last few months in the Bungalow, the hotel -- the motel known as the Bungalow, that he had been working there as a messenger. He was a bit angry at them. He said that -- that they had exploited him, that he had to light a fire for them, that he had to clean and brush their shoes and boots, that they treated him unkindly. I had the impression that he was very indignant about them. They asked him -- they went on to ask him, "Who is in the Bungalow? Who were the people doing this?" And he said that it was full of troops, soldiers, that the units for special purposes were stationed there, Anto Furundzija was there, that Kraljevic came often, that Miroslav Bralo, known as Cicko, could come often, that Cerkez would sometimes stop by, as well as Vlado Santic, that he would see him going there often too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did he say anything about the events of the day before the attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, they asked him, and I was interested in hearing. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: He was where?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In the Bungalow motel, on the 15th, the day before. He said that -- that there was intensified activity with arming, equipment, fresh forces were coming in. There were many of them, a lot of them. He also said that in the evening, at what time was it, after 11.00 or around 11.00 p.m., I can't remember exactly, but in the evening, he said that Santic arrived there in a car, Santic Vlado, that he had brought with him a parcel or a crate of alcohol, that there had been a meeting there which he did not attend, of course, because he was not planned for it, but he heard -- overheard a few things. Then he was asked what it was that he overheard, and he said, "I heard Vlado Santic saying that the order was that not a single male from 12 to 70 years of age must remain alive, and everyone else should be captured and taken somewhere." Where, I don't know, I can only assume and he didn't say. He didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate of how old this Zoran Santic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I know it's been recorded, but maybe 14. About 14. I'm not sure, but he was young.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Mr. Santic, Zoran?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Afterwards, I didn't attend the further interrogation. He was in the fire brigade centre. And what happened with him later, I don't know. I don't know when he was released. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, were you -- did you remain in Stari Vitez for a period of time after the attack?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Were you there on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall anything happening on that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I remember and everyone remembers, whoever was in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In the afternoon there was a powerful explosion, due to which the house we were in shook, as did not the whole of Stari Vitez, I would say the whole of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At some point did you go out and survey the damage?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Not immediately, but I did later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to display the three photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think Prosecution Exhibit 63, we have only a Xerox of the original photograph, if I'm not mistaken, and we will replace that with true photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you look at Prosecution Exhibit 63 and tell us what that depicts?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. This is the place in Stari Vitez where a tank blew up. It was full of explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: The translation I got was "tank". Are you referring to a military tank or some sort of a truck? Do you not understand my question? What was your understanding that blew up on the 18th in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: On the 18th. It was a tank truck for fuel, for petrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And does Exhibit 63 show what you saw in Stari Vitez following that explosion?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could we have the next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And could you tell us what Exhibit 64 shows?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This is the day when UNPROFOR -- may I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: When the tank truck exploded in this part, this house, which used to be here, simply -- that was a big house, it had a first floor, and it simply disappeared. There was a basement in the house, then there was a floor, and because of the shelling and the snipers which shot from all sides, the people went into the basement of the house; and when this tank truck here (indicating) blew up, the house was blown away, and this concrete floor dropped onto the people. There were seven or eight people inside the house in the basement, and this concrete slab fell on top of them. At first, we could hear them begging for help, asking for air. In some places, you could see a hand sticking out, but this did not go on for long. And then the people died because no one was able to remove this concrete slab. Then UNPROFOR arrived, and this shows UNPROFOR removing the concrete and pulling out the people, and I was standing over there on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did they pull out the people alive or dead; do you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What is your understanding of how this truck bomb was accomplished? Was there anyone in the truck, for example, when it went off; and if so, do you know who?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: According to data we received later on, we learned that the tank truck had come from the direction of the Catholic church and that it had passed through Vitez, through Stari Vitez. The driver was a Bosniak, whom I don't know personally, but we know that he was a refugee, a refugee from somewhere in Krajina. I don't know exactly where. He had been driven away by the Serbs. They used various means, such as opium, to drug him, leaving him with barely enough strength to hold the wheel. His hands were tied to the wheel. We presume that the gas had been pressed down with something to accelerate, and since we didn't pay any attention to that road, the tank truck passed through, and it was only after it blew up that we closed off that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And again, Exhibit 65, if you could quickly just identify that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Again, this is in Stari Vitez. Some IFOR units and some local people are looking for corpses and clearing up the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Vitez, and could you just quickly tell us how you left it?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I remained in Stari Vitez 25 days, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Why didn't you leave earlier? Why couldn't you leave earlier?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I think that's clear. I have already said that we were surrounded on all sides, encircled. There was HVO everywhere. They were firing at us with rocket launchers, machine guns, mortars, all kinds of weapons, and we couldn't move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How did you finally get out after 25 days, I think you said? How did you finally manage to get out of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I left Vitez in an UNPROFOR personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: While you were in Vitez and before you left, did you participate or have any knowledge of the burial that occurred on April 28th?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, I was there in Stari Vitez that day. I was still in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What was your role in the burial, if any?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I didn't have any role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know who was being buried on that day in Stari Vitez, not by name but from where they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where were these bodies coming from?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: They were -- you mean where they used to live?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That's right, where they used to live.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Where they were killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That's right, where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Most of these people were from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I just have two more photographs. One is already an exhibit, P --

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Just a moment. There were people from Ahmici, but there were also people from the town, the town, the centre of Vitez, because there were quite a lot of murders in the buildings, in the flats or apartments in the centre of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You yourself didn't actually witness the burial, did you, on April 28th?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: You mean was I there? Was I present?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: On the field where the burial took place, yes, were you present there?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was that your choice, not to be there?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can the usher now show P24, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Exhibit P24 has been placed on the machine. Is that a picture of something that you can recognise and, if so, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: These are members of the HVO with this vehicle, and this gun with four barrels on the vehicle, these are the barrels of an anti-aircraft gun, an anti-aircraft gun, I mean 20-millimetres calibre, is loaded with this equipment, and they went around with it. They didn't conceal it in any way. They always used it to demonstrate their strength like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When you say "they went around with it, they didn't conceal it," who is the "they" you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: They, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So just to be clear, did you yourself see weapons like that in and around the Vitez area during this time period that we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you ever see an anti-aircraft weapon either like that or different than what is depicted in this picture in and around the Ivo Papic house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was it the same as this picture or was it different, and if it's different, how?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This weapon, I saw this weapon once when Darko Kraljevic surrounded and occupied the Ministry of the Interior with his unit. The vehicle was later parked in front of the municipality building. Nothing was concealed. They showed it quite openly. This truck was yellow, the driver -- I don't know his name, but I know the driver by site, he's from Mosunj, and he would often stay at the cafe where I stayed. It was called Babica Kafana. They had a tall TAM, blue in colour, which used to be a PAM, Browning 20.7 millimetres -- 12.7 millimetres, sorry, or they would have an anti-aircraft gun like this but with only three barrels, and the driver of the TAM was called Vrebac, was his second name, and they called him Cicak. I don't know what his real name was. They also had a white vehicle on which there were five barrels, a rocket launcher -- multiple rocket launchers, 22, I think, and the driver of that truck was called Nenad Palavra.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of these weapons that you've just described around the Ivo/Dragan Papic house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Which one or ones did you see around his house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I saw the blue TAM, the blue one with the PAM. It used to be a PAM. Sometimes there was a PAM on it and sometimes it was simply covered over with a canvas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This TAM, was it smaller than what is depicted in this picture, the same, or larger?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It was a little smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you recall where, in relation to the Papic house, did you see this anti-aircraft weapon? Was it in the front yard, was it in the back yard, or on the side of the house, or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: When I was on my way to Ahmici, I saw this TAM vehicle with an anti-aircraft machine gun on it, and it was immediately after the first conflict. It was positioned on the country lane, and the anti-aircraft machine gun was pointed toward Ahmici; and on one occasion, I saw this TAM covered over with a canvas, and they were unloading something from it. I know they were crates, military crates, used in the military for transporting ammunitions or other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Staying with this TAM for a moment, you mentioned a country lane where you saw this TAM. Where is this country lane in relation to the Papic house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I can show you on the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit 30, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Exhibit 30, is this the picture you were referring to that you wanted to see?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This is a photograph that you've previously identified showing the house of Ivo and Dragan Papic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Show us, if you can, on that picture where you saw that anti-aircraft weapon that you've described already?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: (Indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you do that again, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: (Indicates)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That would be what looks like a driveway alongside the Papic house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, this is the road leading toward the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I have one more photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Maybe I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I have one last photograph to show.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you identify that, please, Exhibit 66?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What does that show?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This is the religious building of the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you see --

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The religious building of the Bosniaks in Ahmici, the mosque near the school. This is the mosque built by the late Hazim Hadzi, and this was done by extremists, the extreme HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You see the writing on the main part of the building?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: To the left of the window?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that says, please?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It's the name of their operation on the 16th of April when they started out. It was called "48 Hours of Ashes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is that what that says on the mosque, "Disco" ...

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It says "Balija," which is a derogatory name for the Muslims, it says "God," it says "48 Hours of Ashes," it says "Disco," and they made a disco which opened its doors on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And the "48 Hours of Ashes" is a term you have come to associate with the attack on April 16, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: For the information of the Court, this picture was taken in, I believe, 1996, and we have no information as to who put those words on the mosque, but the phrase "48 Hours of Ashes" is the phrase that has been associated with this attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, one last thing we need to do. You've spoken at length about --

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This must not remain unexplained, when you say that there is no proof who has done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Go ahead and explain.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: One thing is true, that this has not been written by the Bosniaks because at that time, they were not allowed to enter the village, so this was written by the Croats. There was graffiti like this on other houses too all over Ahmici. This year the Bosniaks returned and they built a large number of houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I apologise for skipping over that so quickly. After the attack in April of 1993, were there any, to your knowledge, any Bosniaks left in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Not in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Who were the only people left in Ahmici after the attack in 1993, to the best of your knowledge? Not by name but by religious and ethnic association.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: As far as I know, and as everybody knows, everybody knows that only the Croats remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've spoken about Dragan Papic at length. Could you look around this courtroom and see if you can identify anyone who is or looks like Dragan Papic? Can you see him in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, I can see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And can you tell us where he is?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In the last row, first there's Santic and then Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you distinguish between the two people, Santic and Papic, just by description of their face? Does one have facial hair and the other not, and if so, which one is which?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: We cooperated and we know one another from these contacts, and what do I have to say? Papic has a small beard, and Santic has no beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And may the record reflect that he has identified Santic and Papic. You've also mentioned in your testimony Zoran Kupreskic. Do you see him in the Court room today?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you describe where he is sitting now?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The first row, the first on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And may the record reflect that he has identified Zoran Papic, although maybe we should be a little more specific -- sorry, Zoran Kupreskic. The person you're identifying as Zoran Kupreskic, does he have a moustache only, or does he have a moustache and a beard?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: He has a moustache and a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If the record can reflect that he has identified Zoran Kupreskic. Finally, you've mentioned Vlatko Kupreskic. Do you see him in the Court room today?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where is he sitting and how is he dressed?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: He is the third in the first row from the left, and the third from the right or the second from the left. He's wearing a tie, a white shirt, he is clean shaven, no moustache, no beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May the record reflect that he has identified Vlatko Kupreskic. At this point we would pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moskowitz. Before we break for coffee, may I ask Mr. Pavkovic if he has AN idea how many legal counsel would like to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that it will take at least one hour for the cross-examination, and the attorneys are attorney Petar Puliselic, attorney Ranko Radovic, attorney Borislav Krajina and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We break now for coffee and we come back in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, I once again forgot to offer the exhibits officially into evidence. I would like to be able to do that now. I was also notified during the break from one of the interpreters that she felt there had been a misinterpretation on a question. I can clear that up now or do that on redirect, whichever you think is preferable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Maybe later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness, I could offer then, at this moment, Exhibits 62, 63, 64, 65 and 66. Sixty-two we're offering under seal. Those are the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence? So they're admitted into evidence. Yes Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Defence counsel have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we may start with the cross-examination. Mr. Puliselic

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have two or three brief questions whereby we might reveal the identity of the witness, so could I ask for a closed session for those questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we now go into closed session? (Closed session).

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the date when the Territorial Defence developed into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us that date?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It depended on the area in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It depended on the progress made with the formation of the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in any event, in Vitez, on the 1st of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Are there some generalised dates, a date that is celebrated as the date when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that is?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It is the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us how many statements you have made so far in connection with the events linked to Ahmici, and whom you made those statements to?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I have not made many statements. If you're saying something, you must be sure of what you're saying, as I wasn't in Ahmici on that day. I avoided entering into any polemics, or analysis or debate with people who were victims of that act.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't think you understood me. My question was how many statements you made to official bodies who were investigating those events?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I understood you, I just wanted to say this by way of introduction. Officially only statements linked to the Tribunal, and that was on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: A couple of occasions. The Defence have your statement from 1998, to be more precise, from the 9th of March, 1998, which you made to the investigator of the International Tribunal. Can you tell me whether six years after the event you really do recall all the details that you have described?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Let me be quite precise. Everything they asked me here today I was able to answer, and I did. The things that I couldn't remember and that I didn't know, I didn't answer those questions, nor can I answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me, please, where you were when you heard that a checkpoint had been set up in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Again, you have to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: The checkpoint that you said had been established later, after the first conflict, near Ivo Papic's house.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I must ask you to be precise, because there were checkpoints very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But the checkpoint you spoke about today.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Very well then, yes. That's okay then. Where was I was the question. I was in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: At your workplace? Where were you in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez in the headquarters, the defence headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: And what happened then? Who informed you of this?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The information? The information came from people who were coming from the direction of Busovaca and Zenica, or who were trying to pass either, or from people who were above that spot on a slope, at a height so they can see everything that is happening down there. And I also said that I had been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Could you explain, in slightly more detail, what this checkpoint looked out at? What was it? What was there? What kinds of obstacles? Were there any mines, landmines? What was around this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. There is a turning to the left, going to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: From which direction?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: When you're coming from Vitez, because I mostly came from the direction of Vitez. And before turning for Ahmici there is a double bend, and as soon as you pass the bend you see the road turning left to Ahmici, and a little further forward there is a widening of the road for the bus to stop, and that was where the checkpoint was. These were the usual type of checkpoints. They all resembled one another in those days. They would use those metal cross-bars that were positioned across the roads so that if a vehicle were to pass, it could pass only if it went zigzag around those obstacles. So right of the checkpoint there was a -- I wouldn't call it a bunker, but an ordinary shelter made with sandbags. And there was, as I have already said, or if I didn't I'm saying it now, there was a machine gun, a light machine gun, an M-72 there. Then there was the sign with the word "stop" on it, and to the left and the right there were soldiers. And the road going to Ahmici, there were obstacles across the road with building blocks. So probably when they passed in they would just move a building block and pass and then put the block back in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there, roughly, and did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Let me see. There were three there, and three over there, and two over here. About eight. I knew Vinko Vidovic, Sacko Vidovic, I don't know his proper first name. He was young when I'd left. I didn't recognise the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In view of the fact that so much time has elapsed since that event, are you quite certain that this event linked to this roadblock was after the first conflict or perhaps was it before the first conflict? I'm referring to the conflict of the 20th of October. Are you quite sure this occurred after this conflict?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: After, though there were barricades, as I said, even before. Then they would be removed, and after this one there was another one and it was removed, but this is the one that is important today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: That is precisely why I'm asking you whether you're quite sure whether this roadblock was before or after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how Dragan Papic was dressed when you saw him? I'm asking you this because in this part of your testimony there's a difference between what you said today and what you told the investigators. You are now claiming that he had a black jacket and a camouflage vest, whereas earlier on you never mentioned this black jacket. So I'm wondering where the addition came from. Can you explain that? Earlier on you said he was wearing a camouflage uniform, and that on top of that he had a blue jacket. That is what you told the investigator. So how come there's a difference now?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't see that that's a problem. What is important is that he was in uniform. And when they asked me, they didn't insist on me saying anything in particular. I just said he was in uniform. After that, I gave more thought to the whole situation, so that these details came back to me, and what I said I abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said that Dragan Papic was the commander, in your assessment, of the checkpoint at that time near his house?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure of that or is it just an assumption of yours?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Let us start from my assumptions and then the factual evidence. My assumptions were first those when I came, and if soldiers stopped me and detained me until he comes, and then he says that I can't pass but that I have to go back, then that is my assumption, that he's the commander. And secondly, I think I said that I went with Santic, and that Nenad Santic told me, in so many words, that we're going to see the commanders in the field. He said that we would be going to visit them in their homes, and he was leading me. I just followed him. So this is the evidence which I am presenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that it was the Muslims who, long before the first conflict that occurred on the 20th of October, 1992, had put up a roadblock? Are you aware of that when this happened?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I apologise. Are talking about Muslims or Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Bosniaks, as we are a nation. A barricade that was put up before the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes, much before. Maybe a whole month before.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In the same spot. Yes, there was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Why was it erected on the part of the Bosniaks and when was this?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it did exist. That is why I said that there were many barricades, and this was the only one which the citizens, the people, the people of Ahmici, the civilians, there was not a single rifle, they just stopped the traffic there, blocked the traffic. The traffic was blocked because at the checkpoint in Dubravica, they were turning back all the Bosniaks. They wouldn't let anyone pass to Vitez or to the factory. They confiscated everything that they could take away. So this was a kind of revolt that had prompted it, but this barricade didn't stand there for more than two hours. We dealt with it immediately, because maybe 50 metres ahead the Croats placed their own barricade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: In connection with that barricade, in the same spot that you referred to a moment ago, saying that the HVO had put up the road block, did Cerkez and other persons participate in those negotiations, because the Defence has certain information to that effect, that this had to do with the removal of the barricade erected by the Bosniaks. A meeting was held and there were negotiations.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: They did take place then as well, because the Croats put up another one, but the difference was that the Croats came out with rifles and they threatened with an armed conflict. So we went there again, only this time there was Marijan Lucic, at the time he was in command of the police, and again there was Santic, and it was quickly resolved and the roadblock was removed, so there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: So you were present?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know the members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina called Sadik and Sujo Ahmic, Nisvet and Fikret Ahmic, and person by the surname of Hrustic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it slowly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I will repeat it. Sadik and Sujo Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Sadik? No. Maybe another name, whom I presume --

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Sujo?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Sujo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Muso and Fikret Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: A person with the surname of Hrustic?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, there were many people surnamed Hrustic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But was there a Hrustic at the barricade on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the members of the B and H army manning the barricade shot at a person who passed around the barricade in a car, and that they would stop the cargo vehicles and confiscate the food that was being transported in these vehicles? Were there any complaints, and do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: First of all, sir, there was no army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were no members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina anywhere at that time in that area. No one came out with a rifle, no one stopped a single truck, especially if it was transporting food.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Where exactly was the light machine gun you referred to? Was it on the road near the roadblock you talked about, or was it positioned by the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: It was by the side of the road to the right where there is a widening for a bus stop, and it was facing Ahmici, which is very important. It was pointed toward Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: In your statement today, you say that it was taken away somewhere into the house or around the Papic house. You didn't mention this in the previous statement that you made to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Perhaps they didn't ask me about that. I only respond to questions I'm asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: There is another discrepancy in what you say. You told the investigator that on one occasion between the two conflicts, behind the house or in the back yard of the Papic house, you saw a truck with an anti-aircraft gun while now you say that this was a TAM vehicle with a light machine gun and that it was in the driveway or, rather, on the road leading into the yard.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, it's maybe a matter of the way the question is put and the translation, but what I said today is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please, because I have forgotten what you said about the number of barrels in that weapon. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I believe that you've forgotten it, but if I haven't forgotten it when it was six years ago, I'm afraid I've forgotten what I said an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: That's very strange. Can you say how many barrels there were?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: You mean what I said here today? It was a semi-automatic machine gun. Many people mix this up with a PAT, and I said it was PAM 12.7 millimetres. I think I've said everything now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you say, since you passed by frequently, whether you saw Dragan Papic firing from any kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I didn't pass by daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You passed by often.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, often, but not every day. And secondly, you are talking a lot about these weapons. I said that they would put away one weapon and put up another weapon, so other people saw the PAT. I didn't see the PAT, I saw the PAM. The PAT is an anti-aircraft gun and the PAM is a light machine gun, and I saw the light machine gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness, could you please answer the question put to you by Defence counsel, whether you saw Dragan Papic firing from any kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said that ten days before the first conflict, together with Pero Skopljak and other people, you held talks with several people to negotiate peace and that you went to Dragan Papic's house. What did Dragan Papic say to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: That statement is not well-founded. I didn't say that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I didn't say that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I'm simply asking you what Dragan Papic told you when you were in the house when you were going around with all these people to talk about peace.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: You mentioned Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to hear, you were accompanied by Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: There were several visits, but the one made with Nenad Santic was the one connected with the resolving of the situation. We sat down, we had a normal conversation. He promised -- we were told that there would be no problems, that the people could come back and everything would be all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any members of the household present on that occasion, from the family?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Ivo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You mean the father?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. Ivo Papic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigator, you said that a young HVO soldier happened to go into Stari Vitez by accident and that he was taken prisoner by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and questioned, and we mentioned this today.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of the persons who questioned him?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I can, but in a closed session, in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will go into a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Witness B, do you know what happened to this young man, this --

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Because the Defence has information that this young man's name is actually Zoran Vidovic, that he was not a soldier of the HVO, and that he was 16 years old, and that after this interrogation, he was never seen again, and also that his body was never found. Do you know anything about this? Have you heard anything about this event? Did you hear about it later?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, no. Zoran Santic was because, as I have already said, I left in a personnel carrier and this went on for another year, but we had no further contact with that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know, in this period in October 1992 until the 16th of April, 1993, on how many occasions roadblocks were erected by the Bosniaks on that part of the road?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: From when?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: From the period we discussed today, before the 20th until the conflict on the 16th of April, 1993, so it's a precise period.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, it's very hard to make estimates because things are much more profound.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The permanent checkpoints were manned by the HVO. We tried, in all kinds of ways with the commanders of the HVO, to make sure that there were Bosniaks at the roadblocks as well, that there would be two Croats and two Bosniaks at each checkpoint, but this never actually happened. The first time we tried, it was in Dubravica. There was a Croatian flag at the checkpoint. Our men put up our flag with the lilies, Cerkez came, and they pulled down the Bosniak flag. There was never a Bosniak checkpoint in the direction of Busovaca. From Dubravica to Travnik, at one time there was a checkpoint near Grbavica, the village of Grbavica, for a time. It didn't last long. And there was a Croatian checkpoint, a second one, a third one, five or six checkpoints toward Novi Travnik. The only checkpoint we set up was at Grbavica, but it only lasted for 15 days or less. There was a lot of pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Who set up the barricade on the 20th of October, 1992? At whose orders was the roadblock set up?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The barricade?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 20th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Well, near the cemetery, the Catholic cemetery at Ahmici, on the road.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This was not a proper barricade. It was only an ordinary obstacle, the aim of which was to stop or slow down the movement of the Croatian army from Kresevo, Kiseljak, Busovaca, around two and a half thousand of them armed to the teeth with guns, bombs, grenades, who had set out to Novi Travnik to kill Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to again answer the question? The question was: Who gave orders to set up the roadblock, barricade, whatever, on the 20th or 19th of October, 1992? Could you please answer this question?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: In Vitez, in the school, there was a defence headquarters, the commander was Sefkija Dzidic, and other people who took part in the process of decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many villages in the Lasva River Valley were attacked by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992? Serbian villages or Croatian, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Let me repeat. There was no army there, and if there is no army, what can you use to attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Well, you told us when the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was set up.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the area of Vitez, was established on the 1st of December when a brigade was established -- or it may have been the 12th of December. In any case, it was December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Was there a plan of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to cut off the Vitez-Busovaca road at Ahmici? Can you tell us briefly whether you know of this, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a plan which the same army had to take over the explosives factory in Vitez? Do you know anything about this or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I know everything. There was never a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic, a general of the army, in his book "Cunning Strategy," says there was a plan. Have you heard about this book?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't read it. Sefer Halilovic was in Sarajevo, and he may have thought later that there was something, I don't know what he thought, but I know that he did not know what was going on on the territory of the Vitez Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had black uniforms? Do you know of the Black Swans unit?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I think that this question has nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you this because black uniforms are mentioned so often, so was there a unit of this kind and did it have black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I would like to concentrate on the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you this question. Can you tell me "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please say "Yes" or "No." If you say you don't know, you can say "I don't know," but otherwise, you should answer.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Yes, I know. The Black Swans unit existed as a unit of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the name "Black Swans" did not mean that they were wearing black uniforms. They only had a patch on their sleeve showing a black swan because their first commander was nicknamed "Swan" and the unit was named the Black Swans after him, and the uniform was a camouflage uniform like the other B and H uniforms. It was never a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a cooperation of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HOS and their cooperation over a certain time period? Do you know when this existed?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Can you be more specific? Can you tell me the time and the place you are referring to because I want to answer questions about Vitez and Ahmici, because if we start talking about Croatia or Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Well, Bosnia and Herzegovina is a State. I can't say what was happening in Herzegovina. I'm talking about Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Simply say "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: About the cooperation, all I know is that at the beginning, the HOS had some ideas which overlapped with the standpoints of the army until Kraljevic was murdered in Herzegovina and the 11 or 12 others who were killed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know about the event in the Mahala in Stari Vitez when a shell was fired at the part of the town inhabited by the Croats? Do you know how many children were killed on that occasion who were playing in front of their houses?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I think that at this court, if I have taken an oath to tell the truth, I would like your questions to be well-grounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this event, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I don't want to answer this question because you say this shell was fired from Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As I say, could you please say "Yes" or "No"? If you don't know, we will move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours. I'm trying to say that this shell, if it fell, it couldn't have been fired from Stari Vitez because Stari Vitez did not have that calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But the fact is that a shell did hit the Croatian part of Vitez and eight children playing in front of their houses were killed, so surely this was not fired by an HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: This was later when the war was in full swing. Where the shell came from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did members of the Vitez TO or, rather, of the military police, in the course of 1992, enter houses of citizens without any legal reason?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: Members of the HVO military police did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: My question has to do with members of the Territorial Defence and the military police within the Territorial Defence. Do you know that, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: That they entered Croatian homes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness B
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's too late to start with Mr. Radovic, so we will continue tomorrow. However, before we adjourn, let me express the concern of the Court about the slow pace of our proceedings. For instance, today the Prosecution had estimated about one hour for the examination-in-chief of this particular witness and it took about three hours or more. I wonder whether we could try to find ways and means of speeding up our proceedings? Otherwise, it will take more than two months for the Prosecution case. All right. So we will adjourn now and we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
